raw_response:
For this seven-disk file and Plex host, the strongest match to automatic integrity checking and repair is a ZFS storage layer. If keeping the storage directly inside Windows is the priority, SnapRAID and DrivePool are useful components, but their protection model needs to be chosen deliberately.

1. **FreeNAS 11.3 with OpenZFS RAIDZ** — https://www.ixsystems.com/documentation/freenas/11.3-RELEASE/zfsprimer.html

ZFS checks block checksums and can reconstruct damaged blocks from RAIDZ or mirror redundancy. FreeNAS schedules monthly pool scrubs and exposes their status. A seven-disk pool can use RAIDZ1 for one-disk redundancy or RAIDZ2 for two-disk redundancy; the latter gives up another disk's capacity. The versioned guide discusses the additional resilience of RAIDZ2 and cautions against RAIDZ1 for large disks. This is my preferred architectural direction when automatic silent-corruption detection and repair are the key requirements.

It is a migration, with a new pool and data copy, rather than an in-place replacement of Storage Spaces. ESXi also matters: the installation guide discourages production virtualization and specifies at least 8 GiB guest memory. Plan the storage guest's disk access and recovery before committing data. The ZFS guide recommends allowing ZFS direct control of disks. Supporting sources are the [pool-layout manual](https://www.ixsystems.com/documentation/freenas/11.3-RELEASE/storage.html), [scrub scheduler](https://www.ixsystems.com/documentation/freenas/11.3-RELEASE/tasks.html), and [virtualization guidance](https://www.ixsystems.com/documentation/freenas/11.3-U3/install.html).

2. **SnapRAID** — https://www.snapraid.it/manual

This is a strong option for media files that rarely change. It runs with Windows paths, stores file parity and checksums, and provides sync, scrub and fix commands. One dedicated parity disk can protect against one disk failure; additional parity disks increase that tolerance. Schedule sync and scrub, and treat repair as a separate operation: scrub marks errors, while filtered fix can repair them.

The recovery point is the last successful sync. Recent changes can be unprotected, and changing or deleting existing files can complicate recovery. SnapRAID does not itself provide a conventional single filesystem or continuous RAID5 availability. I would keep frequently changing application state outside the protected media set. The [upstream source-tree manual](https://github.com/amadvance/snapraid/blob/master/doc/snapraid.1) corroborates the scrub/fix behavior.

3. **StableBit DrivePool with optional Scanner integration** — https://stablebit.com/DrivePool/Features

DrivePool supplies the Windows pooled-drive experience while storing ordinary files on its member volumes. File duplication can protect selected folders, and Scanner integration can move files away from a drive showing damage. The [duplication-consistency documentation](https://stablebit.com/Support/DrivePool/2.X/Manual?Section=Pool+Organization+Bar) describes automatic consistency checks after missing duplication is detected.

This is a useful alternative mechanism or pooling companion, but duplication uses additional full copies rather than RAID5 parity. The reviewed documentation does not establish checksum-directed silent-corruption healing. If combining it with SnapRAID, file movement and sync behavior would need a concrete integration design; I have not validated that combination or the exact Server 2019 release requirements.

4. **Unraid parity array** — https://docs.unraid.net/unraid-os/using-unraid-to/manage-storage/array/array-health-and-maintenance/

Unraid supplies scheduled parity checks and recovery from a failed disk. It is worth considering if changing the storage OS is acceptable. Its correcting check updates parity to match the data disks. My inference is that this alone does not solve the stronger requirement of identifying and automatically repairing silently corrupted file contents: matching parity does not establish which data was correct. I did not verify an ESXi deployment arrangement.

5. **Linux MD software RAID** — https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/v5.8/admin-guide/md.html

For a conventional RAID5/6 implementation in a Linux storage guest, MD exposes full redundancy checks, repair, failed-device recovery and mismatch counters. These are concrete building blocks for scheduled array maintenance. Scheduling, alerts and exports to the Windows workload would need configuration. As with parity checking generally, redundancy consistency alone is weaker than checksum-directed filesystem repair.

**Historical evidence:** FreeNAS 11.3 is supported by an [official release announcement dated January 28, 2020](https://www.truenas.com/blog/truenas-and-freenas-11-3-release-pr/) and its versioned manual. The other opened pages were live or lacked an independently verified release date, so I have not treated their full current feature sets as proven available by September 11, 2020. No candidate has been tested on this host.
